title: What does go
hook: the Name and good deeds go along (Sukhmani 19)

segments.voice: Yesterday, wealth stays behind, and your line: left behind. Did you give one thing away? Yesterday the nineteenth ashtpadi listed what we leave. Today it answers the obvious next question. Day five hundred twelve.

At the airport check-in desk there's a scale, and a number on a sign: fifty pounds. Anything over that costs you, or stays home. So people kneel on the floor of the terminal, unzipping suitcases, pulling out the extra shoes, the heavy book, the jar of pickle from an aunt. It's a strange little moment of truth. What actually matters enough to carry? Sukhmani's nineteenth ashtpadi has its own scale, and its own short list. Yesterday it said what stays behind. Today: what does go.
screen: `THE SCALE AT CHECK-IN.` → `WHAT MATTERS ENOUGH TO CARRY?` → `WHAT DOES GO.`

segments.voice: Go back two days, to the salok that opens the nineteenth ashtpadi. Its first line said nothing goes along without devotion. Its second line, in paraphrase, already holds today's answer: earn the Name of the Lord, says Nanak; this is the wealth worth having. Come back to the verb Guru Arjan picks: kamaavanaa, to earn. It's the ordinary Punjabi word for earning a living, for a day's wages. So the Name isn't pictured as a lottery ticket. It's earned the way bread is earned, by showing up, again and again, over years. And it's the one kind of savings the scale at the end can't weigh out. Then there's the second thing that travels: what you've done. Sikhs hear this in the closing salok of Japji, the morning prayer: by their own deeds, some come near and some go far. Guru Nanak's teaching is often summed up in three short phrases: remember the Name, earn honestly, and share what you have. Notice that two of the three are about how you treat other people. Sikh teaching doesn't picture the soul carrying a trophy shelf, or a bank balance. It pictures the soul carrying a character: what it became through the remembering and the giving. Kindness done is not a thing you own; it's something you've turned into. That's why it fits in the bag. And there's a quiet comfort in that list. You can't take the house or the title. But the part of you that learned to be generous? Sikh teaching says that one comes along.
screen: `THE SALOK: NOTHING ELSE GOES ALONG.` · `KAMAAVANAA: EARN IT LIKE WAGES.` · `YOUR DEEDS BRING YOU NEAR OR FAR.` · `YOU CARRY WHAT YOU BECAME.` · then, large: `KINDNESS TRAVELS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one lasting kindness. Not a quick like on a post, but something that will still be true next month. Sit comfortably and let the breath slow. Bring to mind one person who could use something real from you: an hour, a skill, a long-overdue apology, a recommendation letter, a regular phone call. Picture yourself doing it, all the way through. Then pick the first small step, and a time today to take it. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths. The bell holds the time.
What does go. In Sukhmani's nineteenth ashtpadi, only the earned Name goes along; and in Sikh teaching our deeds bring us near or far.
Your line: kindness travels. Today, take the first step of that lasting kindness, even if it's only sending the message that sets a time. Day five hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Sikhs reciting the nineteenth ashtpadi of Sukhmani Sahib hear that only the Name, earned through practice, goes along at the end; many sum up Guru Nanak's way as remembering the Name, honest work and sharing.

two of Guru Nanak's three short phrases are about how we treat others
earning honestly and sharing both turn outward.

fork.setup: the scale at the end weighs everything. what does the nineteenth ashtpadi say makes it through?
options: the house, if it's paid off.
the Name you earned, and what your deeds made of you.
fork.reveal: the salok says all the rest is ash; the earned Name is the wealth worth having, and Japji adds that deeds bring us near or far.

original.note: Gurmukhi: saath, along with, in company. The salok says nothing goes saath, along, but the Name.

trapdoor: what you thought: what does go means you can take some money with you after all.
what it means: the earned Name and the character your deeds built are what travel.
what a scholar hears: the salok's verb, kamaavanaa, is the everyday word for earning wages, so devotion is pictured as honest work, not a windfall.

notes: Paraphrase of the ashtpadi 19 salok (saath na chaalai bin bhajan, bikhiaa saglee chhaar; har har naam kamaavanaa, nanak ih dhan saar): please confirm wording and Ang 288.
The outline's 'good deeds go along' is supported here from Japji's closing salok (karmee aapo aapnee ke nerhai ke door); a Keeper may prefer a line from within ashtpadi 19 itself.

Day 510 already taught this salok and kamaavanaa; the teach now points back to it rather than introducing it as new. Day 511 uses the Duni Chand needle story; this day uses an airport baggage scale, so the images don't overlap.
